title: How Type-A Are You? Take the Type-A Quiz.
author: Parker Houston
summary: Parker Houston recounts the origin of the Type-A label, coined not by psychologists but by cardiologists Meyer Friedman and Ray Rosenman after an upholsterer noticed their patients wore out the front edges of waiting-room chairs. He summarizes their 1959 study linking Type-A behavior with heart disease, and notes that later research pointed to hostility, anger, and chronic stress rather than the broad label. Friedman himself, a self-described recovering Type A who suffered angina and heart attacks, eventually taught Type-B classes and softened his own conduct at home. Prompted by his own mild cardiac findings, Houston reflects on where he adds unnecessary tension and concludes that the people he leads need steadiness rather than urgency. He closes with a deliberately unscientific, humorous quiz and a question for readers about where tension could be released.
points: The Type-A concept began with cardiologists noticing that patients literally sat on the edges of their seats.
Later research suggested hostility, anger, and chronic stress matter more to heart health than the general Type-A pattern.
Meyer Friedman's own late-life shift toward Type-B habits included no longer criticizing his wife or lecturing his children.
Houston argues that the people he leads need steadiness from him, his family needs presence, and his friends sometimes need him to relax.
quotes: I recently learned the history of the term “Type A,” and I was surprised to discover it wasn’t coined by a psychologist.
The story goes that an upholsterer pointed out something unusual about the chairs in their waiting room: the front edges were wearing out much faster than the rest.

Type-A behavior itself has not been established as an independent cause of heart disease, and subsequent research has suggested that specific characteristics—such as hostility, anger, and chronic stress—may be more important than the broad Type-A label.
He encouraged them to leave their watches at home for the day, drive in the slow lane, read classics, or deliberately choose the longest line at the grocery store.
The people I lead don’t need more urgency from me; they need more steadiness.
Maybe the goal isn’t to stop caring, stop achieving, or stop pushing ourselves to become better.
Maybe it’s learning that not everything needs to feel like an emergency.
